title: Inside-Outside Net: Detecting Objects in Context with Skip Pooling and Recurrent Neural Networks

problem.summary: Accurate detectors such as Fast/Faster R-CNN only use information inside the region of interest and pool from the final convolutional layer, so wider image context and fine-grained multi-scale detail are discarded; this especially hurts small and occluded objects.
statements: Detectors restrict computation to the region of interest and ignore context elsewhere in the image, which limits how ambiguous or occluded objects can be recognized.
Pooling descriptors only from the last convolutional layer discards the high-resolution features that small objects need.
Context and multi-scale cues existed as separate ideas (spatial RNNs, skip layers) but were not combined into a single detection architecture.

evidence.quote: Current state-of-the-art detection approaches [7, 30] only use information near an object’s region of interest (ROI). This places constraints on the type and accuracy of objects that may be detected.
The information gained is especially important for small objects, which require the higher spatial resolution provided by lower-level layers.
In general, small objects are challenging for detectors: there are fewer pixels on the object, they are harder to localize, and there can be many more of them per image.

background.summary: ION builds directly on the Fast R-CNN pipeline and borrows two prior ideas: multi-scale skip-layer features for pedestrian detection (Sermanet et al.) and spatial RNNs for context; it also compares against context-aware MR-CNN and detectors that pool only from conv5.

relatedWork.name: Fast R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: base detector whose pipeline and hyperparameters ION extends
relatedWork.quote: Our experiments are conducted with Fast R-CNN [8], which is an end-to-end trainable refinement of He et al.’s SPPnet [13].

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN / SPPnet
relatedWork.relation: prior detectors that pool only from the last convolutional layer, the limitation ION removes
relatedWork.quote: Recent successful detectors such as Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN [30], and SPPnet, all pool from the last convolutional layer (“conv5 3”) in VGG16 [35].

relatedWork.name: Multi-stage features (Sermanet et al.)
relatedWork.relation: closest prior skip-connection usage; ION adds L2 normalization before combining layers
relatedWork.quote: Our usage of skip connections is most closely related to those used by Sermanet et al. [34] (termed “multi-stage features”) for pedestrian detection.

relatedWork.name: Spatial RNNs
relatedWork.relation: prior mechanism for running RNNs over feature maps, reused here to compute context features
relatedWork.quote: We employ spatial RNNs as a mechanism for computing contextual features for use in object detection.

relatedWork.name: MR-CNN
relatedWork.relation: competing context-based detector and two-round box-regression scheme adopted by ION
relatedWork.quote: MR-CNN also uses context and achieves 78.2%.

evidence.quote: It is well known in the study of human and computer vision that context plays an important role in visual recognition [37, 26, 5].
We demonstrate that both sources of additional information, context and multi-scale, are complementary in nature.

solution.summary: ION adds a 2x stacked four-directional IRNN on top of conv5 to produce context features, and pools each ROI's descriptor from conv3, conv4, conv5 and those context features; descriptors are L2-normalized, concatenated, rescaled and reduced by a 1x1 convolution before the Fast R-CNN classification and box heads.
solution.approach: Four-directional IRNNs supply inside/outside context features while ROI descriptors are skip-pooled and L2-normalized across multiple conv layers.
components: VGG-16 backbone inside the Fast R-CNN framework
2x stacked four-direction IRNN computing context features on conv5
skip pooling of ROIs from conv3, conv4, conv5 and context features
L2 normalization plus learned/fixed per-channel scale and 1x1 dimension reduction
optional semantic segmentation auxiliary loss to regularize the top IRNN
selective search proposals (MCG + RPN mix for the COCO submission)
weighted voting with two rounds of bounding box regression at test time

evidence.quote: Contextual information outside the region of interest is integrated using spatial recurrent neural networks.
Inside, we use skip pooling to extract information at multiple scales and levels of abstraction.
At the top of the network, a 2x stacked 4-directional IRNN (explained later) computes context features that describe the image both globally and locally.
The descriptors are L2-normalized, concatenated, re-scaled, and dimension-reduced (1x1 convolution) to produce a fixed-length feature descriptor for each proposal of size 512x7x7.

experiments.summary: ION is evaluated on PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 and MS COCO against Fast R-CNN, RPN, MR-CNN and HyperNet, with a design study on pooling layers, normalization, segmentation loss, context mechanisms and IRNN variants, plus per-size AP breakdowns and COCO challenge results.

benchmarks.split: 2015 test-dev, same images and schedule as Fast R-CNN baseline

evidence.quote: ION improves state-of-the-art on PASCAL VOC 2012 object detection from 73.9% to 76.4% mAP.
As shown in Table 3, when trained on the same images with the same schedule, our method obtains a large improvement over the baseline with a mAP of 24.9%.
Using only a single model (no ensembling), our submission achieved 31.0% on test-competition score and 31.2% on test-dev score (Table 3).
For COCO, if we look at small3 objects, average precision and average recall improve from 4.1% to 7.0% and from 7.3% to 10.7% respectively.

limitations.summary: ION still depends on external proposals, where selective search is very weak on small COCO objects; headline numbers rely on extra tricks such as segmentation labels, weighted box voting and long schedules, and box voting can even hurt the COCO metric.
items: Proposal generation is a bottleneck: selective search averages under 10% recall on small COCO objects.
Best numbers need SBD segmentation labels, weighted voting with tuned thresholds, dropout removal and long training schedules.
Short training schedules do not fully converge, so results are schedule-sensitive.
Two-round box regression and weighted voting initially reduced COCO 0.5:0.95 performance until thresholds were re-tuned.

evidence.quote: Small objects are even more challenging for proposal methods. For all experiments, we are using selective search [38] for object proposals, which performs very poorly on small objects in COCO with an average recall under 10% [27].
We found that shorter training schedules are not enough to fully converge.
found that performance decreases on the COCO metric (IOU 0.5:0.95, second row of Table 3).

deploymentClaims: 0.8 s per image on a Titan X GPU excluding proposal generation (1.15 s with two-stage box regression).

evidence.quote: taking 0.8s per image on a Titan X GPU (excluding proposal generation) without two-stage bounding box regression and 1.15s per image with it.
